messages:
Miles Thornton: collecting notes for the postmortem doc section: “error budget impact + what would have been blocked under the new tiered policy”. drop specifics here (numbers, gates, mitigations). trying to be concrete, not hand-wavy.

Aisha Bello: numbers (Hosted tier, chat/completions streaming route group):
- SLO target (draft): 99.90% “successful streams” over 30d (excludes invalid auth, 4xx misuse, customer-side timeout)
- budget: 43.2 min / 30d
- during incident window (approx 52 min from first spike to mitigation), effective stream success dipped to ~99.1% for us-east-1 + eu-west-1 combined
- error budget burn estimate from slo-toolkit backfill: ~19–22 min consumed in <1h (aka ~45–50% of monthly budget in one event)
- burn-rate alerts that would have fired under the standard: 1h/6h multiwindow would have paged (we saw it in the scratch alert channel; it was “FYI” at the time)

Rafael Mendes: add color: a chunk of “burn” was streaming disconnect classification being wrong (client abort vs server fault). once gateway hotfix landed, the burn curve changed retroactively. we should call out: “budget calculations pre-fix were pessimistic” + link to follow-up action item.

Amara Diallo: +1. for the postmortem: prior to the gateway change, we were counting a bunch of 499s as server-side disconnects. after PR 18440-style logic, only server-initiated disconnects count against stream success. that’s *why* Support reported “your dashboard doesn’t match what we see”.

Sergio Costa: dashboard screenshots useful:
- hosted burn board (internal): https://console.redwoodinference.com/internal/slo/hosted?route=chat_streaming
- burn peaked at ~28x (1h window) for ~12 min
- budget remaining at trough hit ~49% (30d window)
- alerts in #eng-sre were not paging yet bc we were still “dry-running” the new rules

Sean Gallagher: for “what would have been blocked”: map to the draft policy states:
- State A (healthy): normal releases
- State B (at-risk): canary-only + approvals + no risky toggles
- State C (exhausted): change freeze except mitigations

we effectively would’ve flipped to State B within ~10–15 min of the first sustained burn, and would’ve hit State C if we hadn’t mitigated quickly (based on the burn forecast line Sergio pulled).

Sahana Iyer: re: CI gates (hypothetical but concrete): the gateway deploy that went out 20 min before the spike would have been blocked by the “at-risk” gate in soft-block mode *if* it was running with budgets wired.
- it was a non-mitigation change (timeout defaults tweak + retry behavior)
- canary analysis looked “green” on raw 5xx but budget-aware analysis would have flagged “budget risk” bc stream disconnect SLI was spiking

Connor O'Brien: governance notes to capture:
- under new policy, once Hosted chat-streaming enters “at-risk”, any deploy to gateway/routing/runtime affecting that route requires:
  1) change record link + explicit risk acknowledgement
  2) approval from platform-oncall or SRE oncall (not just codeowners)
  3) rollout must stay canary until burn normalizes (no fast-forward)

we should phrase it as: “would have forced slower rollout + earlier rollback decision” rather than “would have prevented the incident entirely”.

Mina Haddad: routing mitigations that would have been auto-triggered if enforcement was live:
- policy engine would prefer safe fallback model variants (same family) once burn > threshold for 10m
- shift traffic away from affected region when 1h burn-rate crosses X (we’re using 4x / 10m in the draft)
- disable “aggressive batching” profile for Hosted temporarily (we currently do this manually)

in the incident we did 2 of those manually via console + config, just later than ideal.

Logan Wright: observability angle: include note that burn-rate signal was available, but it wasn’t surfaced in the incident channel. incident-bot PR adds posting “budget remaining + burn-rate” to incident threads. that would’ve made the “should we throttle?” decision easier.

incident-bot: (retro summary) Detected elevated SLO burn for Hosted/chat_streaming.
- 1h burn-rate: 27.6x (threshold 14x)
- 6h burn-rate: 8.3x (threshold 6x)
- Budget remaining (30d): 51%
Runbook: https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/x/error-budget-exhaustion

Aisha Bello: what actions would have been constrained (explicit list for postmortem):
- would have blocked/promoted rollout from 10% -> 50% while burn was > threshold (policy: “no expansion during State B/C”)
- would have prevented enabling the new retry policy globally without an override token + audit note
- would have auto-enabled protective throttling earlier (Hosted only) to stop cascading timeouts (we debated it for ~15 min)
- would have forced routing fallback sooner (we waited for manual confirmation)

Rafael Mendes: and what would *not* be blocked (important so this doesn’t read like “policy would stop all work”):
- mitigations: rollback, disabling the problematic feature flag, enabling throttling, region failover, lowering concurrency
- hotfix to correct SLI accounting (that’s a reliability fix)

Sean Gallagher: wording suggestion for the postmortem section:
“Error budget impact: this incident consumed ~half of the 30d error budget for Hosted streaming success in <1 hour (based on current SLI definition). Under the tiered error budget policy, the service would have entered ‘at-risk’ within ~15 minutes, triggering canary-only releases, additional approvals for any non-mitigation changes, and automated routing/throttling mitigations. The key delta is not punishment; it is faster feedback + forced de-risking while burn is elevated.”

Miles Thornton: perfect. i’ll lift the concrete bullets + numbers, and add the caveat about misclassification making early burn look worse. if anyone has a specific “deploy X would have been blocked at Y time”, reply w/ details and i’ll include as an example.

Sergio Costa: example w/ timestamps (approx):
- 09:12 deploy-bot shows gateway config rollout started
- 09:31 burn alert would’ve tripped “at-risk” (1h/6h)
- 09:33 budget-aware canary check would’ve tagged run as “budget risk: high”
- 09:35 policy would have required rollback or override token to continue beyond canary

Amara Diallo: :thumbsup: and add that the classification fix is now part of the SLI spec so we don’t keep re-litigating 499s.

Connor O'Brien: :+1: also mention “override tokens require TTL + incident link” (auditable). that’s a nice concrete behavior change.

Miles Thornton: got it. thanks all.
